title: Logic tells both prisoners to betray, so both serve longer
body: Two suspects held apart can each stay silent or betray the other. Whatever the partner does, betraying shortens your own sentence, so two rational players both betray and serve **2 years each** instead of the 1 they would get by both keeping quiet. Play the game over and over and the picture changes: in Robert Axelrod’s computer tournaments around 1980, the winner was Anatol Rapoport’s **tit for tat**, which stays silent first and then copies the other player’s last move.

slides.question: Your partner is going to stay silent. Which choice gives you the shortest sentence?
slides.explanation: Betraying gets you 0 years instead of 1. And if your partner betrays, betraying gets you 2 years instead of 3. Either way, betrayal is better for you.

slides.alt: Animation in a dark interrogation room: two hat-wearing silhouettes in separate rooms both choose to betray. A payoff board shows why betraying always cuts your own sentence. Then a simulated tournament of five strategies, 200 rounds a match, ends with tit for tat serving the fewest years.
slides.music: “Night on the Docks - Sax” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Years in prison for you, by what each of you does
slides.note: Whatever your partner does, betraying cuts your own sentence by a year

slides.heading: A trap made of logic
slides.text: Mutual betrayal is the game’s only strong Nash equilibrium: neither player can do better by changing just their own move. Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the puzzle at the RAND Corporation in 1950; Albert W. Tucker later framed it as prison sentences.

slides.heading: Play it again
slides.text: Robert Axelrod invited colleagues to send in computer strategies for the repeated game, with each pair playing 200 rounds. Tit for tat, the entry from Anatol Rapoport, was both the simplest strategy and the winner, in both of his tournaments.

slides.heading: What the successful strategies shared
items: Nice: never the first to betray
Retaliating: hits back after a betrayal
Non-envious: doesn’t try to outscore the other

slides.heading: Nice means never betraying first. Nice or not?
slides.explanation: A coin flip may betray in round one. Tit for two tats is even more patient than tit for tat: it only hits back after two betrayals in a row.

slides.heading: Winning without beating anyone
slides.text: Tit for tat only betrays after being betrayed, so it can never finish a match with fewer years than its opponent. In the animation’s mini-tournament it still had the lowest total, by settling into long runs of silence with the strategies that cooperated.
